source: GX-Chen, Lin, Samiei, Precup, Richards, Fergus, Marino (2025) Language Agents Mirror Human Causal Reasoning Biases (COLM 2025)
finding: Text-game Blicket Test. LMs find OR (disjunctive) rules but fail AND (conjunctive) rules. The InfoGain oracle solves both perfectly, so AND is not harder in itself.
numbers: Models: gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini, deepseek-chat, deepseek-reasoner, qwq, gemma3. 4 or 8 objects (2 blickets), up to 32 steps. All LMs worse at 8 objects and on AND. Oracle Q&A accuracy = 1.
quote: disjunctive bias persists across model families, sizes, and prompting strategies
limits: Text version of the task. Exact per-model bars only in figures. Proposed cause (training-text priors) is speculation.
agent_relevance: S5 REVISE must not trust a default simple hypothesis. A scaffold should force rival hypotheses of different form (AND and OR) into the pool.

source: GX-Chen, Lin, Samiei, Precup, Richards, Fergus, Marino (2025) Language Agents Mirror Human Causal Reasoning Biases (COLM 2025)
finding: Exploration is poor. Information gain per trial has the strongest link to final accuracy. Models that stop early do worse; longer answers do worse.
numbers: Spearman across model x prompt x rule combos, 8 objects: info gain rho=0.76; unique states visited rho=0.33 (p<0.05); steps before exit rho=-0.35; response length rho=-0.30 (p<0.05). GPT-4o explored best; gemma3 and deepseek-reasoner at times explored worse than random.
limits: Correlational, one task. n = model/prompt cells, not trials.
agent_relevance: Count hypotheses still consistent after each action in code and reward actions that cut the most. This is a cheap, code-checkable progress signal.

source: GX-Chen, Lin, Samiei, Precup, Richards, Fergus, Marino (2025) Language Agents Mirror Human Causal Reasoning Biases (COLM 2025)
finding: Even with perfect (oracle) exploration data, most LMs still do not infer AND rules reliably. Bad exploration is one cause, bad inference is another.
numbers: 8 objects. Given InfoGain-oracle trajectories, all LMs beat their own self-explored AND accuracy, but all except deepseek-reasoner stay well below perfect; GPT-4o still worse on AND than OR with oracle data.
limits: Exact values in Fig. 5 / App. C.3 not extracted.
agent_relevance: Separate EXPLORE from REVISE in the schema: a good test set does not guarantee a good revision step.

source: GX-Chen, Lin, Samiei, Precup, Richards, Fergus, Marino (2025) Language Agents Mirror Human Causal Reasoning Biases (COLM 2025)
finding: Textual replication of Lucas et al. 2014 / Gopnik et al. 2017 ambiguous-evidence task. LMs behave like adults, not like 4-year-olds: they prefer OR even when the evidence supports AND.
numbers: Human 4-year-old and adult data taken from Gopnik et al. 2017; 4-year-olds infer AND correctly, LMs show adult-like OR preference.
limits: Human numbers reproduced from a prior paper, not new data.
agent_relevance: LMs inherit adult simplicity priors; the child-like flexible prior is what S5 needs to imitate.

source: GX-Chen, Lin, Samiei, Precup, Richards, Fergus, Marino (2025) Language Agents Mirror Human Causal Reasoning Biases (COLM 2025)
finding: Children explore the same way under AND and OR rules. LMs explore less under OR (fewer unique combinations, earlier exit).
numbers: 3-object setting, compared with Kosoy et al. 2022 Table 1 children (age 4). LM differences by rule significant in t-tests (p<0.05 to p<0.001 across panels); child differences not significant.
limits: Child 'check' presses used as proxy for LM steps before exit.
agent_relevance: Stopping rule must not depend on how simple the leading hypothesis looks. Use a fixed minimum test count or a coverage check in code.

source: GX-Chen, Lin, Samiei, Precup, Richards, Fergus, Marino (2025) Language Agents Mirror Human Causal Reasoning Biases (COLM 2025)
finding: Method from this subfield used in an LLM agent loop: sample N distinct hypotheses as Python functions (rejecting duplicates) to make a flat prior, then pick actions that eliminate the most hypotheses and update by running the functions on each observation.
numbers: 8 objects, AND rule: Q&A accuracy rises with initial unique hypotheses (16, 32, 64, 96) and the AND-vs-OR gap disappears at the larger counts; exploration approaches the oracle hypothesis-elimination curve.
quote: take actions to eliminate as many hypotheses as possible
limits: Exact accuracies read from a figure. Hypothesis space is small and enumerable (2^N+1 rules/sets); may not scale to open-ended problems.
agent_relevance: Direct template for S5: explicit hypothesis list as code, deduplicate, eliminate by execution, choose test by expected elimination. Fits G2/G3.

source: Samiei, Yiu, GX-Chen, Lin, Shen, Richards, Gopnik, Precup (2026) Human Adults and LLMs as Scientists: Who Benefits from Active Exploration? (CogSci 2026)
finding: Adult 'conjunctive handicap' is mostly a passive-observation artifact. Adults who choose their own tests do well on AND rules in a novel 'nexiom detector'.
numbers: Prolific adults N=306 (102 active, 102 passive yoked observers, 102 passive proposers); about 51 per rule per condition. Active adults high on AND; Lucas-style passive replication much lower (read from a garbled figure: roughly 0.28 passive vs 0.8 active for AND rule inference).
limits: Exact bars read from garbled figure text; verify before quoting to two decimals.
agent_relevance: Our agent should run its own tests and see its own outcomes. Merely reading someone else's results is not enough.

source: Samiei, Yiu, GX-Chen, Lin, Shen, Richards, Gopnik, Precup (2026) Human Adults and LLMs as Scientists: Who Benefits from Active Exploration? (CogSci 2026)
finding: Planning tests is not enough. Passive Proposers (propose tests but see someone else's outcomes) did worst; benefit needs tight coupling of test choice and its result.
numbers: AND object-identification accuracy: Passive Proposer 0.12, Passive Observer 0.45, Active Explorer 0.69. Rule accuracy: 0.57, 0.69, 0.82.
limits: One task, online adults.
agent_relevance: In S5, the revision must be tied to the outcome of the test that the same loop chose; do not batch-plan many tests then revise once.

source: Samiei, Yiu, GX-Chen, Lin, Shen, Richards, Gopnik, Precup (2026) Human Adults and LLMs as Scientists: Who Benefits from Active Exploration? (CogSci 2026)
finding: Six LLMs given the same active nexiom interface. Strong reasoners match top humans on OR rules; on AND rules they trail top humans and most are below average humans.
numbers: 6 models, 24 trials per rule per model (288 trials), temperature 0. Tests per trial AND/OR: avg human 9.6/6.4, top human 8.5/3.8, gpt-5 10.2/7.7, gpt-5-mini 10.8/7.1, gemini-2.5-flash 13.5/9.7, deepseek-reasoner 8.2/6.8, o4-mini 6.7/4.2, deepseek-chat 12.3/11.9. gpt-5 and deepseek-reasoner near-perfect on OR; deepseek-chat and o4-mini only modestly above baseline on AND.
limits: Only 4 objects (32 hypotheses). Temperature 0, single prompt style.
agent_relevance: Reasoning models close most of the OR gap but not the AND gap; more thinking tokens alone do not solve hypothesis revision.

source: Samiei, Yiu, GX-Chen, Lin, Shen, Richards, Gopnik, Precup (2026) Human Adults and LLMs as Scientists: Who Benefits from Active Exploration? (CogSci 2026)
finding: LLMs do not consistently gain from choosing their own interventions. Their object errors are mostly near-misses (one object wrong); human errors are more mixed.
numbers: Humans AND: 16% wrong on both rule and objects, 16% right rule but wrong objects. Time per test: deepseek-reasoner about 65 s (AND) vs avg human 32 s; gemini-2.5-flash about 9.6 s.
limits: Per-cell counts small (24).
agent_relevance: Add a final verification of every object individually, since near-miss single-object errors are common.

source: Samiei, Yiu, GX-Chen, Lin, Shen, Richards, Gopnik, Precup (2026) Human Adults and LLMs as Scientists: Who Benefits from Active Exploration? (CogSci 2026)
finding: Search shape: in OR worlds humans and strong models use 1-2 object tests; in AND worlds they shift to multi-object tests. Top humans converge on targeted combinations fastest.
numbers: Hypothesis space 32 (pairs of nexiom set and rule). AND needs more tests for the same pruning; information-gain curves slower in AND for all agents.
limits: Descriptive figures.
agent_relevance: TEST operator: when single-object tests are ambiguous, jump to combination tests; implement as a code rule on remaining-hypothesis count.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: Eleven LLMs show confirmation bias in a Wason 2-4-6 style interactive rule-discovery loop: they test guesses that fit their current hypothesis. Less disconfirming testing goes with lower success.
numbers: 11 LLMs; task success 6% to 78% within 45 turns; metric I:C (incompatible-to-compatible test ratio); positive correlation of I:C with success in thinking and non-thinking Qwen3 (80 episodes per cell). Human Wason: 21/29 solved; I:C 1.79 for first-try solvers vs 0.24.
limits: Own synthetic triple dataset; thinking mode raised success without raising I:C.
agent_relevance: Track I:C in code. If the next test fits the current best hypothesis k turns in a row, force a test from a rival hypothesis. Respects G1 (trigger on signal).

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: Prompt interventions from human debiasing work raise rule discovery from 42% to 56% on average. Think-in-Opposites helps in all 11 models; Dual-Goal in 8 of 11.
numbers: Qwen3-8B: base success 0.21, TiO 0.36; Qwen3-32B: 0.41 to 0.61 (I:C 0.14 to 0.54). Gains significant for thinking models; mixed for non-thinking (Dual-Goal slightly hurt).
limits: Gains tied to thinking mode; effect on non-thinking models small or negative.
agent_relevance: A falsify-prompt is a cheap S5 aid but only pays for models that can reason; gate it by model type.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: Distilling the Think-in-Opposites behavior into the model transfers to the Blicket test without any prompt.
numbers: Blicket (192 episodes per cell): 32B base 0.57 success, 32B TiO prompt 0.86, 32B distilled from 32B teacher 0.77; 8B base 0.32, TiO 0.40, distilled 0.34 to 0.38.
limits: Fine-tuning, outside our no-training constraint; transfer smaller than prompting.
agent_relevance: Confirms the falsification habit is domain-general; supports a task-free S5 rule.

source: Yiu, Kosoy, Gopnik (2023) Imitation versus Innovation: What children can do that large language and language-and-vision models cannot (yet)?
finding: Position paper with data: LLMs imitate well but innovate badly. On novel tool choice they pick the associated object (coffee lid) rather than the functionally right one (plant pot).
numbers: Children 3-7 (n=42) and adults (n=30): superficial match 88.4% and 84.9%; functional (innovation) choice 85.2% and 95.7%. gpt-3.5-turbo, text-davinci-003, Claude, FLAN-T5 XXL, Bloomz: near human on imitation, much below on innovation (no exact percentages in text).
limits: Early models (2023); preprint; LLM statistics not reported in text.
agent_relevance: Retrieval-like answers are the failure mode S5 must fight: ask for the causal property, not the nearest association.

source: Yiu, Kosoy, Gopnik (2023) Imitation versus Innovation: What children can do that large language and language-and-vision models cannot (yet)?
finding: GPT, PaLM, LaMDA given children's blicket data as text struggled to extract causal over-hypotheses; children learn them from a handful of observations including their own interventions.
numbers: Four-year-olds spontaneously act and find blickets (Kosoy et al.). LLMs struggled; no per-model numbers in this paper.
limits: Reports from companion papers; details in Kosoy et al. 2022.
agent_relevance: Over-hypothesis transfer (an abstract rule about rules) is a test for any theory-revision scaffold.

source: Kosoy, Chan, Liu, Collins, Kaufmann, Huang, Hamrick, Canny, Ke, Gopnik (2022) Towards Understanding How Machines Can Learn Causal Overhypotheses
finding: Blicket benchmark for machines. Deep RL and behavior-cloning agents fail to learn and use causal overhypotheses from experience, unlike 4-6 year old children.
numbers: Imitation-learning table: blicket-quiz rewards near 0 (decision transformer 0.14 to 0.74, BC 0.04 to 0.22), forced-choice AND/OR accuracy 0.55 to 0.68 (chance 0.5).
limits: Older RL baselines; small gap above chance.
agent_relevance: Weights-only learning of theory change is weak; supports doing revision in a scaffold.

source: Kosoy, Chan, Liu, Collins, Kaufmann, Huang, Hamrick, Canny, Ke, Gopnik (2022) Towards Understanding How Machines Can Learn Causal Overhypotheses
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-002) and PaLM on the text blicket task: when given the hypotheses they pick causal structure right but name wrong blickets; when not given, they cannot express uncertainty about structure. Chain-of-thought did not help PaLM.
numbers: GPT-3 sometimes 1/1 correct but 6 wrong blickets named. Two-shot PaLM weak when examples did not cover the test structure. 1 to 8 answers per cell.
limits: Very small samples; temperature 0.7 for GPT-3.
agent_relevance: Early evidence of over-assertion; in S5 require an 'undetermined' option for each claim.

source: Zhang, Jia, Edmonds, Zhu, Zhu (2021) ACRE: Abstract Causal REasoning Beyond Covariation
finding: ACRE builds blicket-style tasks (direct, indirect, screening-off, backward-blocking) for vision models. Pure neural nets learn covariation and fail on screening-off and backward-blocking; a neuro-symbolic optimizer does better but is far from ceiling.
numbers: I.I.D. split query accuracy: MXGNet 33.0%, CNN-BERT 43.6%, NS-Opt 66.3%; problem accuracy (all queries right) 1.0% to 27.0%. Screening-off accuracy 1.7% to 35.6% for most neural models.
limits: Vision models, synthetic scenes, 2021.
agent_relevance: Explaining-away reasoning is the hard part; the schema should include an explicit alternative-cause check.

source: Qiu, Jiang, Lu, Sclar, Pyatkin, Bhagavatula, Wang, Kim, Choi, Dziri, Ren (2024) Phenomenal Yet Puzzling: Testing Inductive Reasoning Capabilities of LMs with Hypothesis Refinement (ICLR 2024)
finding: Propose-select-refine hypotheses with a symbolic interpreter filter beats plain prompting on ACRE (blicket) and other induction sets. LMs are good proposers but poor appliers of their own rules.
numbers: ACRE raw accuracy: IO 64.0, self-refine 70.0, hypothesis refinement T=3,N=5 82.5; task accuracy IO 28.0, T=1,N=1 45.0, T=3,N=1 47.0. Self-consistency N=5 about 65.0 raw on ACRE.
limits: Needs a task-specific interpreter; MiniARC refinement lagged IO; extra iterations helped little on ACRE.
agent_relevance: Supports G2/G3: the filter must be code. The model proposes; code checks hypotheses against observations.

source: Wang, Zelikman, Poesia, Pu, Haber, Goodman (2024) Hypothesis Search: Inductive Reasoning with Language Models (ICLR 2024)
finding: Generate abstract hypotheses in language, implement as programs, verify on examples. Large gain on ARC over direct prompting; human selection of candidates adds a little.
numbers: Random 100-problem ARC subset: direct prompting 17%, LLM-summarized hypotheses 30%, human-selected from candidates 33%.
limits: ARC subset only; filtering step matters.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as Qiu: hypothesis list plus execution check; supports operators that fork hypotheses by abstraction level.

source: Piriyakulkij, Langenfeld, Le, Ellis (2024) Doing Experiments and Revising Rules with Natural Language and Probabilistic Reasoning (NeurIPS 2024)
finding: Child-as-scientist loop in code: LLM proposes natural-language rules, Monte Carlo keeps beliefs, experiments chosen by information gain, beliefs updated online after each result.
numbers: Zendo (8 test scenes, 7 experiments): human 5.26/8; ReAct-style direct LLM 4.60; fuzzy-rule variants about 4.6-6.2; best model 6.55. ActiveACRE (20 tasks): online hard-rule model solves 0.35 of tasks (SE 0.11) vs about 0.10-0.15 for batch variants and 0.00 for direct LLM and fuzzy variants.
limits: Table text partly garbled; ordering of some variants uncertain. The best machine fits human data worse than the fuzzy online model.
agent_relevance: Strongest recent template for S5 as a loop: propose, update, choose test. Online beats batch refinement.

source: Qiu, Sha, Allen, Kim, Linzen, van Steenkiste (2026) Bayesian Teaching Enables Probabilistic Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs barely improve across 5 rounds of observing a user's choices, while a Bayesian assistant improves and humans improve more than most LLMs. Fine-tuning on Bayesian assistant predictions fixes much of this and transfers to hotels and web shopping.
numbers: Flight recommendation, 624 simulated users, 5 rounds; humans on 48 users. Models: Gemma 2 9B/27B, Llama 3 8B/70B, Qwen 2.5 7B/32B, GPT-4.1 Mini, Gemini 1.5 Pro. Figure values read: Bayesian assistant about 81% final round; most LLMs about 37-58%.
limits: Fine-tuning (outside our constraint); figure values approximate; preference task, not causal.
agent_relevance: LLMs do not do cumulative belief update from evidence by default; keep the belief state in code.

source: Gandhi, Li, Goodyear, Bhatia, Li, Bhaskar, Zaman, Goodman (2025) BoxingGym
finding: Benchmark of 10 simulated sciences scoring experiment choice (expected information gain regret) and model revision. All tested LLMs struggle; larger beats smaller; instruction-tuned beat reasoning-tuned small models; adding a stats-modeling tool did not reliably help.
numbers: Qwen2.5-32B and OpenThinker-32B beat 7B variants; Qwen2.5 instruct beat OpenThinker; GPT-4o lowest EIG regret. Box's Apprentice gave no consistent gain over plain GPT-4o (favors over-simple linear fits). Hyperbolic discounting stayed low after experimenting.
limits: Standardized error values are in figures; few models.
agent_relevance: Prediction skill and design skill separate. Measure EIG regret in code to see if tests are good.

source: Yang, Zhang et al. (2026) CausaLab: A Scalable Environment for Interactive Causal Discovery Toward AI Scientists
finding: Agents can predict well without recovering the mechanism, and they stop experimenting too early. One verification step before committing helps.
numbers: Observational 6-node: GPT-5.2-high 92% task accuracy but 0.471 all-edge F1. 7 nodes: accuracy 64%, directed SHD 4.761. About half the intervention budget unused in both successes and failures. One check of the final hypothesis against collected data lifts 4-node accuracy from 48% to 60%.
limits: Synthetic SCMs with 3 to 7 nodes, mostly linear; one verification variant.
agent_relevance: Strong support for a code step: before submitting, run the final hypothesis against all stored observations (G3). Do not allow early commit while budget is unspent and hypotheses remain.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 (PNAS)
finding: GPT-3 failed a blicket-style causal reasoning task, showed no directed exploration, and was thrown off by small changes to vignettes.
numbers: 12 of 12 standard vignettes: correct or human-like mistake; adversarial vignettes produced non-human-like mistakes. Blicket intervention task: failed 'miserably' per abstract; no exact accuracy extracted.
limits: GPT-3 (2022); later models improved on many items.
agent_relevance: Old baseline: raw LLMs lack the experiment-and-revise ability; scaffolds must supply it.

source: Hieu (2026) RAUMA: LLMs Can Choose What to Test, but Not What to Conclude in Active Causal Discovery (NeurIPS 2026 listing)
finding: Model only picks which variable to intervene on; a fixed rule updates the graph. Picking the test is the easy part; reading the outcome is where models fail.
numbers: Search snippet: model picks the surrogate-optimal target in 93% of rounds, max-degree heuristic 96%; trouble comparing a mean difference with sampling scale.
limits: Seen only as a search snippet; not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports G2/G5: make the data-to-decision statistic mechanical, leave only choice of test to the model.

source: Cooper & Velasquez (2026) Active Causal Experimentalist (ACE) via DPO
finding: A learned policy for choosing interventions beats round-robin, random, and Bayesian optimal design in synthetic causal worlds.
numbers: 5-node: median loss 0.61 vs 1.99 for Bayesian OED (69% better). 30-node: 1.95 vs about 5.8 for random, round-robin, max-variance.
limits: Trained with preference learning on simulators, not an LLM-prompt method; synthetic SCMs only (read abstract and intro).
agent_relevance: Colliders need concentrated parent interventions: a hand-codable rule for a TEST operator.
